items.title: Endless pile of Needle In Haystack games begins to emerge, as viral hit imitator's devs claim their code was nicked by a genAI-using clone
items.author: Mark Warren
items.summary: In a metaphor far too on the nose to turn into any form of fiction, at least without the writer getting mercilessly cyberbullied, a game about finding a needle
items.text:
In a metaphor far too on the nose to turn into any form of fiction, at least without the writer getting mercilessly cyberbullied, a game about finding a needle in a haystack has now become the genuine needle at the heart of a pile of imitators. A pile so large, in fact, one copycat game stands accused of ripping code from another.

NoGlyph, developers of Needle In A Haystack, have claimed that their code's been nicked by A Game About Needle In A Haystack devs Little Field Studios. The former game was released on September 29th this year. The latter came out on October 16th. Both offer players a chance to go hunting for metal implements in piles of horse food, and both appear to have been inspired by the as-yet unreleased Needle In A Haystack Simulator, which gained notoriety after serving as the basis of a viral tweet in August.

These are just three of the needle-in-haystack games which've massed on Steam since that clip got a bunch of eyeballs, as various people look to fill the world's apparent desire to hunt stiching implements on a farm.

"Yesterday, on October 16th a game called 'A Game About Needle In A Haystack' by Little Field Studios came out on Steam," a Needle In A Haystack dev called Jahvin wrote in a Steam post over the weekend. "It contains code copied from our game. To be clear, this is about our actual code, not a similar idea or similar mechanics.

"The haystack in our game, meaning how it's drawn, how you dig into it and how gold, lapis and diamond hay work, is something that took a long time to get working properly. When we looked through their game's files, we found 13 of our classes inside it with the exact same names. More than half of the functions in that part match ours exactly. Some of our own error messages are still in there word for word, including one that points to a shader from our project that doesn't exist in their game.

"The copied code matches the versions of our free demo we put out on September 20 and 21, a few weeks before their release. From what we can tell, the rest of their game (the art, the sounds, the other systems) is their own work. Our problem is the hay code."

So, not an apparent copycat calling out another apparent copycat solely for its premise, but an accusation that things have evolved to the point of a studio directly ripping specific code and assets. The Needle In A Haystack devs added that they've filed a copyright notice with Valve and saved off a copy of their findings as proof.

A Game About Needle In A Haystack, the accused, boasts a genAI disclosure in its Steam description, but this only makes clear that the tech was used to produce the game's logo. If the hay code situation is as Jahvin described, that could suggest the potential for AI-assisted decompilation to have been at play in the alleged copying, but there doesn't seem to be any definite confirmation of that as of writing.

Dev concerns about AI being used to easily replicate games have been on the rise, following the recent boom in genAI-assisted decompilation. Just last week, the makers of a game called Drunken Goddess Reflux announced they'd cancelled plans for a public demo in favour of limited-access playtesting sessions, citing concern that "the demo's content could be used to quickly imitate or replicate the game's presentation and gameplay with AI or other tools, and that such works could be released before our launch".

Honestly, I'm just terrified that the ever-growing mound of needle-in-haystack variants will eventually grow to the point of causing Steam's vast barn of games to burst, sending horse-shaped westerns, pitchfork-shaped fantasy RPGs, and water trough-shaped games aimed at thirsty horndogs flying across the plains of the net.

items.title: “Tulsa King,” and Stallone, Start to Show Their Age in Season 4
items.author: Clint Worthington
items.summary: Of the universe of Taylor Sheridan AARP-for-aging-’80s-guys dramas aimed squarely at the silent majority, “Tulsa King” is by far the most charming. Flitting
items.text:
Of the universe of Taylor Sheridan AARP-for-aging-’80s-guys dramas aimed squarely at the silent majority, “Tulsa King” is by far the most charming. Flitting somewhere between “Yellowstone” and “Get Shorty” in its tale of a New York goombah (Sylvester Stallone) starting his criminal enterprise all over again in Oklahoma, the show has spent three seasons simply letting its bulging cast of characters engage in soap-opera theatrics, squaring off against rival gang members and, in this last set of episodes, a vindictive bourbon distiller played by Robert Patrick. (Spoiler alert: Sly burns him at the stake in the season finale. I guess it’s the only way to be sure with the T-1000.) But in season four, “Tulsa King” finally feels like it’s getting lost in the literal and metaphorical sauce.

After taking over Patrick’s distillery, Dwight “The General” Manfredi (Stallone) is finally ready to legitimize his enterprises (well, some of them) and settle down with his girlfriend of three seasons, Margaret Devereaux (Dana Delany). Unfortunately, mysterious circumstances arise at the end of the season premiere that leave Dwight in deep mourning and unsure where his businesses stand with the government. That latter concern is compounded by the elevation of lieutenant governor Amanda Clark (Gretchen Mol), a by-the-books do-gooder who knows Dwight’s game and wants to shut him down permanently, to the top office.

That’s not Dwight’s only concern, of course; his old mafia family in New York City keeps gunning for the profits he’s been building in the Southwest, especially now that his old nemesis, Quiet Ray (James Russo), is fully in charge. What’s more, a greedy German AI tech bro (Flula Borg) is threatening to take Margaret’s horse ranch by eminent domain to turn the land into a data center.

(L-R): Scarlet Stallone as Spencer, Martin Starr as Bodhi, and Jay Will as Tyson in Tulsa King, episode 1, season 4, streaming on Paramount+, 2026. Photo Credit: Steve Swisher/Paramount+

All these conflicts and more stud “Tulsa King”‘s new season, and that’s not even getting into Bodhi’s (Martin Starr) flirtation with wine forgery, or Tyson’s (Jay Will) burgeoning rap career. And let’s not forget Dwight’s unsteady alliance with government spook Musso (Kevin Pollak) from last season and how that dovetails with Dwight’s existing animus with fellow capo Bevilaqua (Frank Grillo). Hey, there are a lot of aging character actors to pay; we gotta give them something to do, right? We should be thankful Samuel L. Jackson isn’t here to soak up more screen time, as he’s supposedly off building his own spinoff down in New Orleans.

“Tulsa King,” at this point, is more overstuffed than a turducken, with a cast so bloated that the gang is juggling at least three or four different schemes at once. Even Sly is getting a little tired; sure, some of that is Dwight’s puffed-up grief, but some of it is the older actor slowing down. (The show even writes a cane into Dwight’s ensemble; it’s passed off as an occasional knee injury that flares up from time to time, but I get the feeling that cane’s here to stay.) Even Sly coasting is compelling enough to watch, but you can tell the rest of the cast has to shore up their game to help carry this thing. This is especially true of Annabella Sciorra’s Joanne, Dwight’s enterprising sister and partner in crime, who slowly becomes the show’s heart and soul.

Gretchen Mol as Amanda Clark in Tulsa King, season 4, streaming on Paramount+, 2026. Photo Credit: Steve Swisher/Paramount+

In fact, you get the most enjoyment from showrunner Dave Erickson and his writing team’s occasional lapses into the ridiculous. Italian enforcer pals Goodie (Chris Caldovino) and Vince (Vincent Piazza) shoot their way out of a white supremacist meeting at a restaurant they happen to be eating at; “You just got robbed by two swarthy Mediterraneans!” they shout as they leave. Dwight mournfully asks an AI chatbot whether God exists, and the scene is treated as if it’s dispensing therapeutic wisdom from on high. Someone gets their head crushed in the jaws of a fossilized dinosaur skull. In these scenes, “Tulsa King” ekes out a kind of campy enjoyment. It’s just a shame you have to sift through so many diluted storylines to get there. (The less said about the budding romance between Garrett Hedlund’s Mitch and Scarlet Stallone’s Spencer, the better.)

It’d be dishonest to claim “Tulsa King” doesn’t offer consistent diversion, even amid the myriad components of Dwight’s business empire and all the spinning plates therein. But this season’s villains don’t compel (including everyone’s favorite “My Son Hunter” director Robert Davi as a creaky enforcer who looks like he can barely stand, let alone take out fools), and so many of the plot threads feel like filler to give Dwight’s bloated entourage things to do. The bulk of the show’s charm falls squarely on Stallone’s broad shoulders, and even he’s starting to lose a step. Here’s hoping the show can get its affairs in order in an already-announced season five, or this vital leg of the Taylor Sheridan universe will go, well, the way of the dinosaur.

Full season screened for review. Premieres October 16th on Paramount+.

MSI Claw 8 EX AI+ specs:

CPU/GPU: Intel Arc G3 Extreme

RAM: 32GB LPDDR5X

Storage: 1TB NVMe SSD

Display: 8in, 1920x1200, 120Hz IPS

Ports: 2x USB-C, 1x 3.5mm, 1x microSD Express

Dimensions: 321x130x48mm

Weight: 785g

Price: From £1,399 / $1,800

Welcome to my review of the MSI Claw 8 EX AI+, a handheld PC that went on sale four months ago. And if you think that’s bad, tell it to the 2025-spec Lenovo Legion Go 2 I’ve left, neglected and unappraised, in the dusty heights of my utility cupboard.

This one, mind, is still worth looking at a smidgen late. It’s the first palmable PC to use Intel’s Arc G3 Extreme SoC, including the Arc B390 integrated graphics that’s already impressed in skinny laptops. Considering both the underwhelming framerate gains of previous handheld chip upgrades, like the Asus ROG Xbox Ally X’s second-gen Ryzen, and the fact that the last-gen Claw 8 AI+ was already a high performer, this here EX model could be the one to usher in a new standard in game go fast technology. Could, and ultimately, does – it’s more than twice as fast as a Steam Deck OLED in some games.

...Which you’d hope, given it costs about twice as much.

You know the routine by now: AI data centres, RAM shortages, component prices, pain. £1,399’s worth, in this case. As a result, the 'AI' in this handheld’s name seems less like it’s advertising a product feature and more like it’s whispering a name in a detective’s ear before passing out from its stab wounds.

It is, at least, intentionally aiming for high-end spec glitz from the off. Hall effect thumbsticks flank a 120Hz, 1920x1200 IPS so vast it overshoots the bottom edge, and inside, that G3 Extreme chip is joined by 32GB of system RAM (might have shaved some 9s of the price with 16GB, but hey) and a nicely spacious 1TB SSD. It’s also, frankly, a lot better-looking than the grey faced Claw 8 AI+, with more rounded grips that sit a little better in the hand. It’s still an unpocketable slab, weighing 785g and stretching nearly an inch wider than its predecessor, but its gamepaddish sculpting does make it somewhat more comfortable to play.

It’s also true that the Claw 8 EX AI+’s pixel-pushing abilities are genuinely top of the line. Even while matching the 1200p resolution demands of other high-enders, it repeatedly biffs them around in Low-quality benchmarks, while making good on a real upgrade on the Claw 8 AI+. Even its smallest advantage, in Black Myth Wukong, will be visibly smoother to a trained eye.

Despite the handheld’s name suggesting some sort of artificially intelligent optimisation is going on, any machine-learned resource-juggling that the Arc G3 Extreme can do is focused on lightweight loads. Its game muscle is, therefore, almost purely thanks to that B390 GPU, which did well in a bunch of other games to boot. Resident Evil Requiem averaged 57fps on Low (with FSR on Quality mode), while Elden Ring usually stayed above 50fps on Medium at native 1200p. Subnautica 2 stuttered a little, but a combination of its Low preset and TSR Quality was enough to get it averaging 56fps.

Next to its Z2 Extreme-powered rivals, and especially the humbler Steam Deck, the Claw 8 EX AI+ is much more likely to enable glossier visual options as well. Big Walk, for instance, averaged 50fps on its High preset, so there’s no urgent need to de-prettify its sunny puzzle island. Forza Horizon 5 also scored 81fps on native-rez High, outspeeding the ROG Xbox Ally X and Legion Go 2 (see? I benchmarked it, before I exiled it) even when they only needed to run on Low.

The best part, as the Claw 8 EX AI+ does still need to be a portable powerhouse, is that its performance doesn’t come at the cost of deafening fan noise or kneecapped battery life. Its cooling setup hums along, not quite silently, but hushed enough to avoid the Legion Go S sensation of gripping a tiny vacuum cleaner. And this is one of precious few handheld PCs able to give the Steam Deck OLED a fight on longevity: Valve’s machine still handles low-demand games better, lasting 5h 48m to the Claw 8 EX AI+’s 3h 37m in Portal 2, though the MSI’s 2h 29m in Elden Ring does edge the Deck OLED’s 2h 14m.

On top of being the most graphically beefy handheld PC on the market, then, the Claw 8 EX AI+ does well on basic usability qualities that too many Windows portables have been willing to sacrifice. On those grounds alone, what else could you call it but the best in its class? Maybe even such that its price, while hardly deserved, is at least understandable?

Even the finest hardware, however, can have an unsanded panel or an exposed nailhead. For the Claw 8 EX AI+, it’s the display that disappoints. Not because it’s bad – in many ways it’s quite a tidy screen, securing its vibrant colours by covering 99% of the sRGB gamut, and having a Deck OLED-beating refresh rate that (for once on a handheld) is paired with a GPU that might actually pump out enough frames to take advantage of it. Even so, the old one was better. In the same tests that snapped that 99% colour coverage, I recorded the Claw 8 EX AI+’s display reaching a contrast ratio of 1,291:1 and a peak brightness of 418cd/m2; as the Claw 8 AI+ hit 1,412:1 and 521cd/m2 in its respective tests, it would appear that MSI have switched to a duller, flatter LCD panel. Even putting aside how the much cheaper Deck OLED remains more vivid and inky than both, if this was an attempt at keeping the Claw 8 EX AI+’s price down, it clearly didn’t work.

Then there’s Windows. Ohhh, Windows, you never learn, and apparently handheld manufacturers don’t either. While SteamOS continues to gorge itself on user-friendly features, designed and tuned specifically for the hardware formats it appears on, Windows 11 remains deflatingly awkward as a portable operating system, still requiring regular touchscreen intervention to navigate. Even using Xbox Full Screen Experience, the more thumbstickable skin Microsoft began stretching over Win11 last year, the Claw 8 EX AI+’s software spat out multiple bugs: my Steam notifications would appear in the middle of the screen, rather than tucked away in the corner, and Cyberpunk 2077 mysteriously lost the ability to run in Fullscreen mode. Most annoyingly, Xbox FSE itself would lag on startup, robbing the Claw’s controls of any input response for several worrying moments.

If you’re even entertaining the possibility of blowing £1,399 on a handheld, there’s a strong possibility that you care less about Windows UX and more about big, fat framerates. Which to be sure, the Claw 8 EX AI+ delivers on. The future of fast portables is here, and even with AMD’s promises of new Ryzen chips and FSR 4 support, that future looks awfully Intel-shaped.

What makes the Claw 8 EX AI+ nice to use, though – at least once it finishes waking up – is the lack of friction that comes with that power. It’s quiet, and doesn’t burn out in an hour, and those qualities are what truly mark the handhelds that best understand their own form factor. They’re why I still use my Steam Deck OLED when I’ve got a Legion Go 2 lying around, anyway.

Still, that same lack of friction should really extend to the softer bits. Which is why, and I suspect I’d be saying this even if the Claw 8 EX AI+ was £800, I’d wait until Valve can do what they’ve done for previous Claws: get SteamOS running on it.

items.title: Steam Next Fest Has Become A Massive Disaster And A Grim Look At The Future
items.author: Zack Zwiezen
items.summary: In years past, I’ve enjoyed checking out Steam Next Fests. These regularly scheduled Valve-sanctioned events encourage devs working on indie games to put
items.text:
In years past, I’ve enjoyed checking out Steam Next Fests. These regularly scheduled Valve-sanctioned events encourage devs working on indie games to put together a demo and share it as part of a larger promotion. However, the most recent, currently ongoing Steam Next Fest is a nightmare with thousands upon thousands of demos, many filled with AI slop. At this point, the vibes are completely rotten, and it’s only made me more worried about the future than excited.

In theory, Steam Next Fest should be a great event for developers. A big pile of new free demos for upcoming games attracts many gamers who are looking for the next cool thing. And Valve promotes it with its own big storefront and menus, making it easy for people to quickly download and play dozens of demos and hopefully wishlist and eventually buy some of them, putting money in Valve’s pockets as well as the devs’ and publishers’ own coffers, too. Plus, fans get to play a bunch of free demos, and game critics and content creators get a batch of neat new games to cover while getting a peek at the future. Sounds great!

But this time around, Steam Next Fest features nearly 7,100 free demos. And that’s just far too many free demos for Next Fest to be usable or useful as it once was for so many people.

It wasn’t always like this. In the past, the number of Next Fest demos was smaller. As reported by Game Discover, during the last Next Fest in June, there were around 4,300 demos. In October 2024, there were around 2,700 demos. And back in October 2023, there were around 900 demos. In those days, it was easier to find cool games and for good stuff to bubble up to the surface. As the number has grown, it’s become harder and harder to actually stand out in the pack or find anything in the flood of games. Now that Steam Next Fest has reached over 7,000 demos, it’s just become an overwhelming nightmare to dig through.

That many demos alone would make Next Fest miserable. However, the other big problem with this recent Next Fest is that so many of the demos are AI slop or crappy clones, or were quickly slapped together via vibe-coding. This was a problem last year, and it’s only gotten much, much worse.

I hopped around Steam Next Fest for a bit today and repeatedly encountered games that looked like they had been cranked out by Claude in a few hours. Many games just openly admit in their AI disclosures that vast portions of their codebase and assets were completely AI-generated. To peruse Steam Next Fest right now is to jump into an ocean of AI garbage and slop. It’s depressing, and has killed all my excitement for Next Fest.

I don’t seem to be alone in this reaction. In general, the vibes around Next Fest this year feel especially rotten and miserable. My timeline is filled with devs, writers, and fans who just seem defeated by the flood of Next Fest demos and AI slop. What was once a joyful Steam event that got people talking about upcoming games with excitement is now yet one more example of how everything is being corrupted and ruined by genAI tools and models.

It also really makes me sad that Valve seems uninterested in curation of any kind and instead relies on its users tagging games and its own algorithms learning what people like and hopefully shielding them from the slop. Valve’s chokehold over PC gaming continues to make me nervous, as the company seems completely uninterested in lifting a finger to actually improve Next Fest or stem the amount of garbage that fills Steam every day now. And one of its only real competitors, Epic, is fully embracing AI and vibe-coding, making it a less-than-stellar replacement.

Earlier this month we reached a depressing milestone: More games have already been added to Steam this year than in all of 2025, a trend that shows no signs of stopping. And now that AI coding tools have become even more capable of spitting out “games” and mods at record speed, leading to a huge influx of vibe-coded software in recent weeks, I suspect that future Next Fests will be even bigger and even worse. The future is grim, folks.

items.title: Can AI slop even have an aesthetic?
items.author: Alex Cranz

items.text:
In the early ’80s, Ken Burns developed a marvelous new technique for historical documentaries that seems totally obvious by modern standards. He would shoot video of photos, using the camera to create a sense of movement as he slowly zoomed in and panned and cut quickly from photo to photo with an accompanying narration. His work seemed to bring history alive, using actors and narrators to provide voices for old historical documents. Sometimes, in Fox Nation’s Houdini: Back From The Dead, I can see the future of documentaries like the Ken Burns ones. Fox advertised the documentary as using AI to bring Houdini back to life, and there are moments where you do feel like the dead have been resurrected. Then a Scarlet Johansson lookalike flashes some distinctively ahistorical cleavage to make Houdini’s wife jealous and that marvelous vision of the future of documentaries disappears as neatly as Houdini would disappear an elephant.


It is a perfect example of AI slop, a phrase we like to use for anything that is AI-heavy. Weird microdramas. Karma-farming fake videos on social media. “We are Charlie Kirk.” Yet usually the AI slop is coming from the fringes. People not already working in the entertainment world and eager to get a piece of the profit pie. This is coming from Fox, albeit the right wing news entertainment version of Fox and not The Simpsons-and-FX version owned by Disney. Fox Nation is a streaming service providing curated content for Fox News super fans. AI slop appearing there, a small service with limited content, makes the slop feel even more sloppy. Watching the doc, I could practically hear a cigar-chomping executive shouting “slop em up, boys.”


That’s a shame because occasionally Houdini: Back From The Dead is an entertaining and visually arresting documentary about a man who was constantly forced to reinvent himself when new technology came and changed the whole landscape of entertainment and media. It goes on tangents, including a suggestion Houdini died because he blasphemed God and the spiritualism movement of the 1920s, and those tangents can be wildly entertaining. They just can’t overcome the cynical nature of the whole affair. It isn’t really about Houdini and using new technology to better engage audiences with his story. It’s about having another thing to click on in the Fox Nation app.


Aesthetically, it’s “AI slop.” Technically, “AI slop” isn’t an aesthetic. Artists will (and have) said repeatedly that AI cannot have an aesthetic because it is made by computers, not people. I disagree, largely because we can all see AI slop and say “yup, that’s AI slop.” There is a visual language—only, the visual language of the AI slop aesthetic changes year to year and sometimes month to month. One upon a time, it was badly formed hands and Will Smith merging with his spaghetti. Objects would warp and shift in distinctly uncanny ways and we could feel the AI wrongness. It’s the aesthetic everyone clocked in the opening credits to Marvel’s Secret Invasion back in 2023.


Now AI can do hands and make Will Smith eat spaghetti while doing martial arts, and the aesthetic has changed too. In restaurant menus and church picnic signs, it’s characterized by a kind of visual maximalism. Cheese drips in globs off burgers and classic cars are polished past the point of shine to a haze meant to suggest it’s even shinier. Houdini: Back From The Dead encapsulates the AI slop aesthetic of motion picture in 2026. There’s no big gloopy-but-meant-to-be-enticing drips of cheese, but oftentimes people do seem to have that same haze around them that the classic cars get, and everyone moves, is lit, and acts, exactly like the AI people in commercials on YouTube.


Houdini: Back From The Dead used real actors to play most of the roles and then AI to lay the historical figures over the performance—basically deepfakes. These characters all have lifeless eyes and mouths that are far more animated than the rest of their faces. It can make it feel like you’re mainlining a couple hours of those AI people selling supplements on YouTube between episodes of hoof-trimming videos. AI-resurrected Harry Houdini is frequently the worst offender. The conceit of the series is he is being interviewed, through the power of AI and possibly God, so the doc frequently cuts to an interview with him where he stares into the camera with soulless blue eyes and a winning smile.


Houdini: Back From The Dead


The likenesses of random celebrities haunt the entire project too. Whatever AI models were used to create this miniseries were clearly trained on modern cinema so extras don’t just look like randoms, they look like Scarlett Johansson or Henry Cavill. Sometimes they look like the AI equivalent of that one female model Pixar uses for every major human female character in its films.


The lighting is the most egregious offender. AI slop in 2026 has a bad habit of giving everyone an ethereal glow that cannot come from the actual visual light sources. Even though most of us can’t tell a key light from a fill light, we know bad lighting when we see it.


There are a surprising amount of scenes with well-deployed genuine historical footage. Harry Houdini happened to be part of the very first plane crash caught on film and the series recreates the incident, cutting between footage of the actual crash and an AI reimagining that escapes the slop aesthetic. As a man dangles from a rope 10,000 feet in the air his plane crashes into another, sending him swinging right into the propeller that he narrowly avoids. The footage, pulled from Houdini’s 1919 film The Grim Game, has deteriorated with age and it can be hard to make out just how dangerous the stunt is, but the AI interjections work, yanking us back to 1919 and a stuntman narrowly avoiding losing his life to a plane propeller. It was the moment that really made me think of Ken Burns, imagining what someone who genuinely cares could do with this technology and a bit of time.


It’s oddly heartening that this Fox Nation miniseries, created so Fox can keep its tiny handful of viewers engaged in a world where Tubi, Pluto, and YouTube exist for free, manages to pull off a sequence like the plane crash one. It is a slop documentary made for the sake of the slop, but it still accomplishes something cool. In the hands of someone not just trying to ride the AI hype train, it could be a genuine tool for good storytelling. In the hands of Ken Burns, this same technology could produce a masterpiece. But it isn’t magic, despite the claims in the trailer. It’s still AI slop, which has a curious (debatable) aesthetic but is never going to be a reason to subscribe to a streaming service.

blocks.x: In the early ’80s, Ken Burns developed a marvelous new technique for historical documentaries that seems totally obvious by modern standards. He would shoot video of photos, using the camera to create a sense of movement as he slowly zoomed in and panned and cut quickly from photo to photo with an accompanying narration. His work seemed to bring history alive, using actors and narrators to provide voices for old historical documents. Sometimes, in Fox Nation’s Houdini: Back From The Dead, I can see the future of documentaries like the Ken Burns ones. Fox advertised the documentary as using AI to bring Houdini back to life, and there are moments where you do feel like the dead have been resurrected. Then a Scarlet Johansson lookalike flashes some distinctively ahistorical cleavage to make Houdini’s wife jealous and that marvelous vision of the future of documentaries disappears as neatly as Houdini would disappear an elephant.

It is a perfect example of AI slop, a phrase we like to use for anything that is AI-heavy. Weird microdramas. Karma-farming fake videos on social media. “We are Charlie Kirk.” Yet usually the AI slop is coming from the fringes. People not already working in the entertainment world and eager to get a piece of the profit pie. This is coming from Fox, albeit the right wing news entertainment version of Fox and not The Simpsons-and-FX version owned by Disney. Fox Nation is a streaming service providing curated content for Fox News super fans. AI slop appearing there, a small service with limited content, makes the slop feel even more sloppy. Watching the doc, I could practically hear a cigar-chomping executive shouting “slop em up, boys.”

That’s a shame because occasionally Houdini: Back From The Dead is an entertaining and visually arresting documentary about a man who was constantly forced to reinvent himself when new technology came and changed the whole landscape of entertainment and media. It goes on tangents, including a suggestion Houdini died because he blasphemed God and the spiritualism movement of the 1920s, and those tangents can be wildly entertaining. They just can’t overcome the cynical nature of the whole affair. It isn’t really about Houdini and using new technology to better engage audiences with his story. It’s about having another thing to click on in the Fox Nation app.

Aesthetically, it’s “AI slop.” Technically, “AI slop” isn’t an aesthetic. Artists will (and have) said repeatedly that AI cannot have an aesthetic because it is made by computers, not people. I disagree, largely because we can all see AI slop and say “yup, that’s AI slop.” There is a visual language—only, the visual language of the AI slop aesthetic changes year to year and sometimes month to month. One upon a time, it was badly formed hands and Will Smith merging with his spaghetti. Objects would warp and shift in distinctly uncanny ways and we could feel the AI wrongness. It’s the aesthetic everyone clocked in the opening credits to Marvel’s Secret Invasion back in 2023.

Now AI can do hands and make Will Smith eat spaghetti while doing martial arts, and the aesthetic has changed too. In restaurant menus and church picnic signs, it’s characterized by a kind of visual maximalism. Cheese drips in globs off burgers and classic cars are polished past the point of shine to a haze meant to suggest it’s even shinier. Houdini: Back From The Dead encapsulates the AI slop aesthetic of motion picture in 2026. There’s no big gloopy-but-meant-to-be-enticing drips of cheese, but oftentimes people do seem to have that same haze around them that the classic cars get, and everyone moves, is lit, and acts, exactly like the AI people in commercials on YouTube.

Houdini: Back From The Dead used real actors to play most of the roles and then AI to lay the historical figures over the performance—basically deepfakes. These characters all have lifeless eyes and mouths that are far more animated than the rest of their faces. It can make it feel like you’re mainlining a couple hours of those AI people selling supplements on YouTube between episodes of hoof-trimming videos. AI-resurrected Harry Houdini is frequently the worst offender. The conceit of the series is he is being interviewed, through the power of AI and possibly God, so the doc frequently cuts to an interview with him where he stares into the camera with soulless blue eyes and a winning smile.
Houdini: Back From The Dead

The likenesses of random celebrities haunt the entire project too. Whatever AI models were used to create this miniseries were clearly trained on modern cinema so extras don’t just look like randoms, they look like Scarlett Johansson or Henry Cavill. Sometimes they look like the AI equivalent of that one female model Pixar uses for every major human female character in its films.

The lighting is the most egregious offender. AI slop in 2026 has a bad habit of giving everyone an ethereal glow that cannot come from the actual visual light sources. Even though most of us can’t tell a key light from a fill light, we know bad lighting when we see it.

There are a surprising amount of scenes with well-deployed genuine historical footage. Harry Houdini happened to be part of the very first plane crash caught on film and the series recreates the incident, cutting between footage of the actual crash and an AI reimagining that escapes the slop aesthetic. As a man dangles from a rope 10,000 feet in the air his plane crashes into another, sending him swinging right into the propeller that he narrowly avoids. The footage, pulled from Houdini’s 1919 film The Grim Game, has deteriorated with age and it can be hard to make out just how dangerous the stunt is, but the AI interjections work, yanking us back to 1919 and a stuntman narrowly avoiding losing his life to a plane propeller. It was the moment that really made me think of Ken Burns, imagining what someone who genuinely cares could do with this technology and a bit of time.

It’s oddly heartening that this Fox Nation miniseries, created so Fox can keep its tiny handful of viewers engaged in a world where Tubi, Pluto, and YouTube exist for free, manages to pull off a sequence like the plane crash one. It is a slop documentary made for the sake of the slop, but it still accomplishes something cool. In the hands of someone not just trying to ride the AI hype train, it could be a genuine tool for good storytelling. In the hands of Ken Burns, this same technology could produce a masterpiece. items.title: Masahiro Sakurai Says Gaming Needs Originality Or It ‘Will Die Slowly’
items.author: Alicia Haddick
items.summary: For the last 16 years at Tokyo Game Show, Masahiro Sakurai has handed out awards centered on game design to celebrate games that do things differently. This
items.text:
For the last 16 years at Tokyo Game Show, Masahiro Sakurai has handed out awards centered on game design to celebrate games that do things differently. This year, however, was the final year for this event, and in a new interview, he shared a somewhat bleak reflection on the importance of originality as he discontinued the prize.

Sakurai’s Game Designers Award was centered on promoting original game design ideas, regardless of sales performance. Winners of the award, not necessarily limited to a single game each year, have included the original Life Is Strange, Mario Kart: Home Circuit, Viewfinder, and Scribblenauts. However, during his speech at the awards show last month, he painted a somber picture, lamenting, “Though it may sound rather grave, originality doesn’t actually have a strong impact on sales. I think it actually ranks low on the list of priorities for many.”

He compared the problem to the way the novelty of a limited-time drink flavor might fade after it’s been released, although he hopes the games industry hosts enough creative minds to avoid this problem. “There likely aren’t many people who try every single new drink that comes out at convenience stores as soon as it’s released. The more you become accustomed to something, the more you gravitate toward the familiar. Most people tend to only want a taste that matches their preference and is exactly what they expect. But an industry that loses that sort of originality will only die slowly. The industry exists today because there have always been new ideas and experiences, and people making them.”

Reflecting further on the comments in an interview with Denfaminico Gamer, he brings up the design philosophy he brought to creating Kirby and Super Smash Bros. In both cases, their respective genres—2D platformers and fighting games—already existed, but by focusing on new ways to let players act and interact in these genres, the games stand on their own. Yet coming up with original ideas and conveying this to an audience today is more difficult than ever, he admits.

“The first important thing is whether or not you can come up with an original idea,” explains Sakurai. “You might be able to expand on the concept of improving upon an existing idea, but when it comes to creating systems without an easy comparison point, who comes up with that idea? Then, you have to get staff to understand that idea, and it’s difficult to convey that ‘this is why it is fun, because you can do this.’ If you’re a game publisher, it’s difficult to then share that big picture. What are the game’s selling points?”

He continues, “Nowadays, so many games are described as XX-like, or games that resemble another one. In other words, the thing everyone else already wants. But originality means you have to create something that isn’t already what people are after, and be deliberate with that. It’s a high hurdle.”

Something AI only exacerbates, he says. When he first opened the award in 2010, there were only roughly 275 games sold on Steam in a given year, a number now at over 19,000. There are over 8000 titles in this month’s Steam Next Fest alone, many vibecoded with AI and reliant on copying existent ideas.

According to Sakurai, this only makes original ideas more important. “Although 19,000 titles is a lot, I think that number will only grow from now on, because AI will be used to turn them out. Most of them will end up unplayable, and there will be so many that it’ll be impossible to keep track or even understand them. With those AI games, the vast majority will be direct copies of games we’ve seen before. There’s already many of them, even now.

“A little while ago, there was a game called Librarian. It’s a game set in a magical world, where all the books have been jumbled up and you have to put them back. That’s the premise, but the mechanics are simple. So, unsurprisingly, a lot of imitators soon followed. Games like Supermarket Chaos or Needle in a Haystack Simulator have multiplied like crazy. They’re all puzzle games, but that kind of imitation will be simple for AI to conduct. But even if AI can create all these sorts of works, such as by analyzing the atmosphere of games from Fumito Ueda like ICO and Shadow of the Colossus and using that to create something similar, which could happen, but AI would not be able to create whatever Ueda himself will create in the future.”

In other words, though Sakurai fears for the future of game originality, if pioneers of game design continue to find the space to create original ideas, then the game industry will persevere. Even if he will no longer present the award he founded, his hope is that originality will find space to thrive. Simply because, without it, there may not be an industry left.

items.title: Final Fantasy Resonance Feels Like Comfort Food, But I Want Cuisine
items.author: Kenneth Shepard
items.summary: Whether or not Final Fantasy Resonance, the new reimagining of the now-defunct Brave Exvius mobile game…resonates with you will probably depend on when you
items.text:
Whether or not Final Fantasy Resonance, the new reimagining of the now-defunct Brave Exvius mobile game…resonates with you will probably depend on when you started playing Square Enix’s long-running RPG series. Though Square Enix says it wants the game to be a potential entry point into a franchise full of them thanks to its anthology format, after putting about a dozen hours into the game, I feel like it’s the kind of nostalgic comfort food that is mostly for people who grew up during the series’ 8- and 16-bit era rather than something that might pull anyone else in.

After stripping out all the gacha mechanics from Brave Exvius and giving the visuals an HD-2D facelift, Resonance is the kind of thing that some fans, those who miss the simple days of gorgeous pixel art and turn-based battles, are likely yearning for. It also has one of the least engaging stories and casts I’ve ever experienced in a Final Fantasy. Its party is full of some of the most one-note Final Fantasy heroes to ever exist, presented here as living tropes that harken back to the old days when Final Fantasy wasn’t presenting some of the most emotionally resonant stories in the RPG genre, and much of its story reads like a first draft that was never really spruced up.

Resonance is working with the bones of a gacha game that probably had different priorities than creating an engaging world and storyline, so I’m not terribly surprised that the world its characters travel through mostly feels like a generic backdrop, but if you aren’t a diehard for the relatively simplistic trappings of old-school Final Fantasy, I cannot imagine how Resonance would ever be the game to draw you in.

That’s all the more apparent when the most compelling thing about it is also deeply rooted in early Final Fantasy. Most of Resonance’s turn-based battles have you doing the genre-standard stuff of targeting enemy weaknesses and avoiding resistances, but on top of having your usual party of four on the field, you also have Visions, which are manifestations of characters from various Final Fantasy games. You recruit them through what is essentially a quick history lesson and quiz about their respective games, and it’s a fun trip down memory lane seeing footage from various games playing in the background as a disembodied voice tells you about their adventures.

Then, these Visions become an equipable secondary party member that gives you a separate batch of abilities and skills with which to take on enemies. It’s an effective way of letting you mix and match team compositions, perhaps giving characters who might be at a disadvantage against one enemy a different set of tools that could help them gain the upper hand. Plus, you get to see cool pixel art of your favorites like Cloud from Final Fantasy VII and Noctis from Final Fantasy XV hanging out during the battle. Each time they use one of their special moves, a 3D rendered cutaway appears on screen that is cool the first time you see it but which you will skip every other time. Still, the way they can change a team’s composition and open up new strategies is a neat touch that adds some strategy to an RPG that’s otherwise straightforward to a fault.

But my god, it is pretty. I’m honestly annoyed at the cinematic cutaways of old Final Fantasy characters because Resonance looks its best when it’s creating elaborate shows of its stunning pixel art. I’ve been playing on my Switch 2 and it looks great in handheld mode, but now I’m just wishing I had spent all that time playing it on my TV because it is so gorgeous to behold.

Those moments in which Square Enix flexes its sprite work are when I’m most happy to be playing Resonance, a game that otherwise underwhelms me at nearly every turn. Resonance is undoubtedly going to hit for those craving an old-school Final Fantasy experience, and on paper, I’m down for one of those myself. I just wish that Resonance didn’t feel so barebones in between its moments of fanservice.

items.title: "Sexy sorceresses" and "bare-chested fighters": Dragon Age's original artists wanted to base it on Conan the Barbarian, much to the outrage of the designers
items.author: Edwin Evans-Thirlwell
items.summary: Buried in the vast and sooty-fingered Summer Eternal anthology, there's an interview with former BioWare developer and Dragon Age lead writer David Gaider, who
items.text:
Buried in the vast and sooty-fingered Summer Eternal anthology, there's an interview with former BioWare developer and Dragon Age lead writer David Gaider, who is now creative director at Stray Gods outfit Summerfall Studios. The interview is a podcast-length account of BioWare's transformations over Gaider's career, stretching back to Baldur's Gate 2. Amongst other things, it explains why the Dragon Age games feel so different from sequel to sequel.

Gaider discusses the original trilogy's fortunes under RPG-phobic parent company Electronic Arts, commenting that 2009's Dragon Age: Origins made it to release partly thanks to "sunk cost" thinking after EA bought the studio. He also talks about Dragon Age's lack of a properly defined vision, early on, which led to a lot of overcorrection between releases. As regards Origins, there was something of a faction war initially between departments over what exact flavour of fantasy fiction the new RPG should draw on.

"When we started, Dragon Age's big premise was 'it's D&D, but it's not," Gaider began. "We'll just file off the serial numbers enough to make it our own. That was not great because there are different kinds of fantasy."

Specifically, a rift emerged at BioWare between developers who wanted to channel Tolkien, and those who wanted to invoke Robert E. Howard's Conan the Barbarian stories. "If you look back at the E3 Expo, where we announced the existence of Dragon Age, and you watch the video, you will see," Gaider went on (the screening in question was behind closed doors, sadly, so all I can do is point you towards IGN's coverage at the time). "It was mostly made by our art department. They were part of the Conan group. And if you watch it, you'll see sexy sorceresses, the fighter is this bare-chested barbarian riding around… it looks very Conan.

Watch on YouTube

"And that part of the team was determined that their vision was set out," he said. "The design department was mostly like, 'no, this is Lord of the Rings, man, okay? Fuck Conan.' But Art didn't want to listen to us, so we're like 'If you're going to ignore us, we'll ignore you.' And that's really why the Dragon Age that came to be is the way it is. If you look at Dragon Age: Origins, if I said to you, this is the art style of a Conan world with the writing style of a Lord of the Rings, then you'd be like, 'Oh.'"

When teams are at odds in this way, it's helpful to have a third group intervene to thrash out a compromise. The producers, for example. Unfortunately, Gaider continued, Dragon Age's production team had their own wild ideas about the project's direction - they thought it should be Diablo. This did, in fairness, have some kind of unifying effect. "Both the art department and the design department completely ignored them. Like, no, we're not doing Diablo."

Nonetheless, the producers persisted. "They wanted that if you hit creatures, they'd just explode in blood," Gaider said. "We actually had presentations where the people in charge were like, 'Yeah, Dragon Age, we want that the theme is blood! Dripping with blood!' And I'm like, 'That's not a theme.' They did get their way a little bit, Dragon Age was pretty bloody. People did almost explode in blood. We had to tone it down a bit because that just didn't feel right."

I realise there's a serious argument being made here about the necessity of knowing your game's heart, before you commit to knocking out scripts, models and trailers, but I am also having fun imagining the inter-departmental squabbles. I picture Gaider bumping into one of the Dragon Age artists outside an elevator in Edmonton, sometime in 2004. The artist's eyes narrow. "Tell me, David," they growl. "What is best in life?" Gaider's knuckles whiten. "To take the ring to Mordor, throw it into Mount Doom, and hear the lamentation of Sauron," he hisses. At this point the elevator doors open and a producer appears, apoplectic and roaring: "Ahh, fresh meat!"

According to Gaider – who would eventually become "vision keeper" or "educator" for Dragon Age as a series - BioWare did a much better job of getting the band together with Mass Effect, mostly thanks to project director Casey Hudson.

"Mass Effect went through much the same kind of struggle," he said. "It's science fiction. It's 'their Star Wars,' is what that was supposed to be. But there's so many different kinds of science fiction. And they had the benefit that Casey Hudson was the responsible person, and realised sooner than Dragon Age did that we need a singular vision. And he eventually put his foot down and said, 'This is what it is.'

Elden Ring Surprise Update Officially Released

Image via FromSoftware

Published Oct 21, 2026, 5:59 AM EDT

Known as 'Cyberpunk 2077's' biggest fan, Angharad is a Welsh games writer who thrives in anything related to digital storytelling. If a video game explores the intricacies and horrors of womanhood, she is there.
Thanks to previous work at GAMINGbible, GameByte, The Loadout, Game Luster, Angharad has built a strong understanding of both the digital world and what fans want from it and is eager to share her thoughts and expertise with readers.

It may have been almost four years since the launch of Elden Ring, but as with any FromSoftware title, it is set to stand the test of time, with legions of players still descending upon the Lands Between to take on some of gaming's most iconic bosses. With the open-world offering countless replayability opportunities, it is no wonder that gamers are finding new and unique ways to tackle the action RPG, and of course, its modding community have also helped keep the game alive with new and exciting content released on a regular basis.

Here at Screen Rant, our very own Christopher Teuton awarded Elden Ring a perfect 10/10 back in 2022, sharing:

Everything about Elden Ring feels like a celebration of what FromSoftware has accomplished since the original release of Demon's Souls, up to and including Déraciné and Sekiro: Shadows Die Twice. The open world genre is perfect for the developer's penchant for hiding NPCs, quests, and items in obscure and hard-to-reach locations, and the Lands Between have been crafted in such a way that it's nearly impossible to get too lost or overwhelmed at any given moment. Elden Ring is exactly what fans want it to be, and it very likely will become many people's favorite FromSoftware title yet.

Now, over three years on, it seems that even FromSoftware is not giving up on Elden Ring just yet, as Title Update 1.17.2 just launched alongside some interesting patch notes.

Whilst it may not be a major update featuring any content updates (much to our dismay), the 1.17.2 update offers a fix to a visual bug which targeted the Gold Tattoo Chest armor when the Hide Helmet option is on. There was also a bug fix for the Repeating Crossbow Skill, meaning that the left-hand graphics display only when you use this weapon in your left hand and hold Leontiel’s Greatsword in your right.

A bug has also been removed that caused status buildup when firing Piquebone Arrows and Fletched Piquebone Arrows in a certain manner and last, but by no means least, there have also been some adjustments to the text seen in the credits.

Like I said, a very minor update, but no less important if those bugs have been affecting your playthrough. With Elden Ring being a single-player title, and FromSoftware reportedly already turning its attention to other projects, it is unlikely that we will receive any major updates or content drops from this point on. However, it is still reassuring to see that the studio is still working on bugs, no matter how small they may be.

For now, Elden Ring fans can look forward to the upcoming live-action movie adaptation courtesy of A24. Set to hit cinemas and IMAX on March 3, 2028, it is still some time away, but with a stacked cast such as Kit Connor, Cailee Spaeny, Ben Whishaw, Nick Offerman, and more, it is no doubt that one of the best video games of all time is in good hands.

Known as 'Cyberpunk 2077's' biggest fan, Angharad is a Welsh games writer who thrives in anything related to digital storytelling. If a video game explores the intricacies and horrors of womanhood, she is there.
Thanks to previous work at GAMINGbible, GameByte, The Loadout, Game Luster, Angharad has built a strong understanding of both the digital world and what fans want from it and is eager to share her thoughts and expertise with readers.

First launching for the Game Boy Advance back in 2002 and marking the first installment in the third generation of Pokémon games, Pokémon Ruby & Sapphire saw players, once again, go up against the Elite Four and the Pokémon League Champion, all whilst dealing with the ongoing threat of a criminal organization.

Welcoming 135 brand-new Pokémon to the roster, as well as double battles, new abilities, contests, and more, Pokémon Ruby & Sapphire received mostly positive reviews, but as is the case with many entries in the Nintendo franchise, it received criticism over its lack of ambition.

However, over the years, nostalgia has taken hold and now, Pokémon Ruby & Sapphire is remembered fondly amongst the Pokémon classics and, as such, fans are over the moon to hear that the games are set to receive a Nintendo Switch port.

Unlike a lot of the Pokémon classics, Pokémon Ruby & Sapphire is not available to play on the Nintendo Switch or Nintendo Switch 2 at the time of writing. However, this is set to change, if reports are to be believed.

Although the ports may not have been confirmed by Game Freak or Nintendo, many leaks have been released over the past few months. The most important of which was a 30-second clip of Pokémon Ruby & Sapphire in HD shared to a Japanese Pokémon social media account. Not only did this footage look to feature a modern-day remake, but the clip being exactly 30 seconds, which is the amount of time you can record a Nintendo Switch clip for, made fans put two and two together.

Additionally, files referencing Gen 3 of Pokémon were found inside emulator data for Pokémon FireRed and LeafGreen, which could hint at its future arrival.

Now, there is another update, and this time it comes courtesy of Shpeshal Nick on Twitter/X. After reaching out to a "source" back in August, they shared that "the ports of Pokémon Ruby/Emerald/Sapphire are planned for late September/October." However, in a more recent update posted on 20 October, they claim that this timeline has changed.

"Reached out to my source and asked for an update here (because everyone keeps asking me) and it seems this plan has changed," the post reads. "The ports apparently won’t make it by the end of this month. Will try and keep you posted when I get an updated timeline. Sorry to let people down."

Game Freak

It is obviously taking all of this information with a pinch of salt in the first place, but even then, Shpeshal Nick has not yet provided information as to when the release date for the ports of Pokémon Ruby/Emerald/Sapphire will now launch, after many fans believed that they would be released in Fall 2026. When asked if their source had given any indication of the revised time frame, they replied, "Nope, unfortunately."

So, it seems as though we are back to waiting for the highly anticipated Nintendo Switch ports for Pokémon Ruby/Emerald/Sapphire, but with neither Nintendo nor Game Freak confirming their existence at the time of writing, it is always worth it to err on the side of caution with your expectations.

items.author: Coto Academy Staff Writer

items.text:
While Japanese has tons of English loanwords, English actually borrows quite a bit from Japanese as well. Words like sushi, karate, or tsunami are so commonly used that it might be easy to forget that they’re loanwords from Japan.

Let’s discover some common Japanese loanwords in English, covering some of the old and some of the new, but this blog is by no means exhaustive. By the end of this article, who knows? New words are probably being borrowed at this very moment.

Why Do Japanese and English Borrow so Many Words From Each Other?

Since Japanese and English come from very different places with distinct cultures, cuisines, and geographic characteristics or phenomena, the more exposed we are to each other’s cultures, the more new concepts and words we encounter. It makes sense that English would just adopt the words for Japanese food items like “sushi” or “ramen.”

However, the word tsunami is also of Japanese origin. It just so happens that English had no word for huge tidal waves, so it borrowed tsunami from Japanese. Often when a word sufficiently describes something we don’t have a word for, we just adopt it into our language. As you are probably well aware, Japanese quite often does the same.

You’ve probably experienced what could be called the katakana glitch. You see a katakana word, and you just can’t figure out what it is until you mouth it, then you finally figure out that biiru (ビール) is actually “beer”. You probably can think of many more English loanwords in Japanese, such as soccer, or sakkaa (サッカー), and even modern slang like rizz, or rizu (リズ). New words are crossing over, perhaps because the internet and pop culture spread new trends faster than ever before.

Note that this doesn’t always happen; when baseball was introduced to Japan, they made their own word for the sport, yakyuu (野球), which is made up of the words field, or 野 (ya), and ball, 球 (kyuu).

Japanese Loanwords Used in English for Food and Entertainment

In 2013, UNESCO named Japanese food an intangible cultural heritage. The flavors and practices associated with Japanese food are unique. Many of the Japanese loanwords in English reflect that uniqueness. Similarly, many aspects of Japanese entertainment tend to originate in Japan, and the English words borrowed from Japanese show that.

A lot of these loanwords are originally written in kanji, hiragana, or katakana. If you need to review hiragana and katakana, head to this article.

1. Karaoke (カラオケ)

Did you even know this was a Japanese word before Karaoke actually came into contact with Japan or the language? It has roots in the words: kara (空), meaning “empty,” and oke (オケ), meaning “orchestra.” So, together the word actually means orchestraAlso, have you seen anyone do karaoke like the Japanese?

2. Sudoku (すどく)

If you’ve played sudoku and understand it, more power to you. This game and its title originated in Japan in 1984 and have since become very popular worldwide. The su comes from suji or suu (数), meaning number, and the doku (独) means single. The overall aim of the game is to get numbers to appear once in squares in a grid. So literally, the numbers must remain single. Or suuji wa dokushin ni kagiru (数字は独身に限る), which was the original title of the game.

Europeans actually played a similar game in the 18th century. In the 1980s, a Japanese publisher distributed sudoku, which turned into a huge hit and has been popular ever since.

3. Pachinko　(パチンコ)

Hard to spend any time in Japan and not see a pachinko parlor. Pachinko is a kind of pinball game played in arcade games or, more commonly, gambling parlors. Japanese people like to make words that mimic or represent the sound you hear, like the bees buzzing or the snake hissing. The word pachinko is partly made up of a Japanese onomatopoeia. The first part, pachin, is from the sound that the metal pinball makes as it hits an obstacle. The ko is a diminutive suffix that means something like ‘little’.

4. Soy (sauce, beans)

Tofu and miso are obviously Japanese loanwords, but soy? Yes, apparently it comes from しょうゆ (shoyu), which is Japanese for soy sauce. The actual Japanese term for the bean is daizu. Edamame, which are green soybeans, is also commonly used in English.

5. Tamari (たまりしょうゆ)

This one is kind of hip these days. Many recipe bloggers suggest using tamari as a ‘healthy’ alternative to regular soy sauce. Tamari is richer, thicker, and less salty than regular soy sauce, but it is also made from fermented soybeans.

6. Shiitake, maitake, matsutake, and enoki mushrooms (椎茸、舞茸、松茸、えのき)

Did I miss any? Many Japanese mushroom names have been carried over and used as-is in English. The most popular of these might be shiitake, which is often pronounced without the second ‘i’, resulting in shitake.

7. Umami (旨味)

Umami is probably one of the most popular Japanese loanwords in English, being used all the time to describe a distinct savory flavor. This term is a relatively recent adoption into the English language, and it’s somewhat new to Japanese as well.

The word was first coined in 1908 when a Japanese scientist used the word to describe the “5th taste,” which is savoriness. In both Japanese and English, umami generally describes the savory flavor you would find in cooked meats, soy sauce, and mushrooms.

items.title: Mirukashi Salon: An Extraordinary Retreat in Rural Japan
items.author: Alina Joan Ito

items.text:
In an unassuming seaside town in Kyushu, the writer and photographer Prairie Stuart-Wolff has started something quietly extraordinary: a salon where guests are encouraged to fully immerse themselves in nature, feeling the progression of the seasons through minute changes observed every day.

Mirukashi Salon specializes in intimate, food-focused retreats, rooted in the idea of Japan’s 72 microseasons, which span four to five days each. Stuart-Wolff runs it out of a custom-built space in Saga Prefecture with her wife, Hanako Nakazato, who comes from a legendary family of potters.

The facility typically hosts a handful of sessions per year for small groups of visitors, each lasting the length of a microseason. While staying at a nearby hotel, guests harvest their own seasonal ingredients, cook alongside Stuart-Wolff in her purpose-built copper kitchen, dine at local restaurants and visit ateliers specializing in regional crafts, including Nakazato’s own pottery studio.

What began as a personal journey for Stuart-Wolff has rapidly captured the world’s imagination. Last year, Mirukashi Salon was named one of Time magazine’s World’s Greatest Places, and has been covered in major global publications from Afar and Travel + Leisure to Condé Nast Traveler. But its appeal lies less in its accolades than in a philosophy of travel built around slowing down, eating locally and paying close attention to the rhythms of the natural world.

The Story Behind Mirukashi Salon

Nearly two decades ago, Stuart-Wolff left her home in New England to join Nakazato in Karatsu. When she arrived, she had barely any experience with Japanese language or culture. “I met Hanako in the States,” Stuart-Wolff recalls. When she first arrived in Japan, she says, “I landed with a total blank slate of just: Let me see what this place is and what resonates with me. I’m grateful because there’s a little bit of danger to knowing too much; you end up traveling to a country looking for affirmation of what you think you know about it.”

Her entry point into Japanese life was the family kitchen, standing alongside her mother-in-law. The two women connected through washing dishes, preparing seasonal ingredients like wild bamboo shoots and filling the dining table with food they’d harvested themselves. Her mother-in-law would chat away in Japanese while Stuart-Wolff helped intuitively, creating a silent dialect of culinary labor.

“We had this shared focus that allowed us to occupy a space together and be productive without actually needing words,” she reflects. Food became her doorway into both the culture and the family she had married into.

Mapping the 72 Seasons

As Stuart-Wolff’s connection to the countryside deepened, she began documenting her observations online, blogging about the subtle ecological shifts that surrounded her. Over time, she discovered that Japanese agriculture historically observed 72 microseasons (or ko), which divide the year into small increments marked by natural phenomena like “rice ripens” or “wagtails sing.”

“I really latched on to it because it became this beautiful architecture on which I could map my experiences,” she explains. “There’s an enormous shift between when spring starts and spring ends, so this notion of there being much shorter periods of time in which there are more subtle shifts made a lot of sense to me. Every five days, something is changing. The light is changing. The air is changing. Flora is changing.”

Stuart-Wolff’s cadence is remarkably calm and unhurried, and her voice lightens even more when asked about her favorite microseason. “I’m always torn. That’s like being asked who your favorite child is,” she says with a laugh, but ultimately points to mid-April. “In Karatsu, it’s a time when you can fashion a whole meal out of things that you forage. You have bamboo shoots coming up, you have the sansho [Japanese pepper] tree leaves coming out … Maybe you still have a little bit of warabi [bracken fern] out in the fields,” she says. “There’s just an abundance of things growing that you can eat, and you really feel like the earth is so high up again.”

The Partnership at the Heart of the Retreat

At the heart of Mirukashi Salon is an intimate creative partnership between Stuart-Wolff and Nakazato that mirrors a key concept of Japanese cuisine: food and the vessel that holds it are inextricably linked.

“She’s a prolific potter,” Stuart-Wolff says of Nakazato. “Seeing her work sparks new ideas for a way to present a dish I’ve made many times, or even a whole new dish.” Conversely, Stuart-Wolff’s culinary experiments inspire Nakazato to explore fresh ceramic shapes and glazes. “She gets to see her work in use through me, and then sees this brand new audience use it. The comments guests make are often quite inspiring and spark ideas she never thought about before.”

Navigating rural Kyushu as an international, same-sex couple presented its own unique set of dynamics. Unlike Stuart-Wolff’s home state of Vermont, countryside Japan offered little initial context for a queer couple. “My biggest challenge was just visibility,” she explains. “In the countryside, lack of exposure meant there was a lack of vocabulary and understanding. Nobody really could see or infer who I was and why I was there.”

Over two decades, the couple has found a wonderful community in their home of Karatsu. For other queer or foreign creatives hoping to find their place in a traditional community, Stuart-Wolff offers a simple philosophy: “Learn the rules and then break them,” she says. “Spend a good amount of time really understanding the local dynamics, and be as respectful as possible until you feel like you are fluent in the local culture. Then start to bring back the aspects of yourself that you can’t live without.”

Staying at Mirukashi Salon

Mirukashi Salon keeps its scale intentionally small. Public sessions are capped at seven guests and hosted roughly seven times a year, typically during key seasonal transitions in spring and autumn. For travelers seeking a more bespoke experience — couples, families or small groups or friends — private salon bookings are also on offer.

For Stuart-Wolff, this approach honors the true historical meaning of a salon: a gathering where participants and hosts hold equal weight in shaping the environment.

“Each salon session is unique in that microseasons are different every year,” Stuart-Wolff says, “but it’s also unique in that we bring these five, six, seven people together at the table. People are bringing their history, their ideas, their interpretations of what they’re seeing. For me, that’s the point of the program: I present something for people to experience, but they are shaping that as well in their time together.”

In an age of bustling tourism and action-packed itineraries, Mirukashi Salon invites guests to experience travel at a slower pace, turning their attention back to the earth. As Stuart-Wolff reflects, the beauty of the microseasons lies in the familiarity of their annual return, and in the small differences each year brings: “They’re a beautiful way to mark time because it happens every year — there’s a familiarity and a comfort to it, but every year is different. So every year is exciting.”

For those willing to slow down and pull up a chair, the salon gives us a gentle reminder that the extraordinary is always unfolding right in front of us.

items.text:
Welcome to Japan! Along with your first steps in your new life in Tokyo, one of your first priorities is to start learning Japanese. Some of you might already have a certain level of Japanese ability, such as reading and writing hiragana and katakana. But what if you have never learned Japanese before?

When you have completely zero knowledge of Japanese, we recommend you join what is called a Japanese Crash Course, like ones offered at Coto Academy. In 4 weeks, you will learn the fundamentals of Japanese, directly useful for your daily life, including an introduction to hiragana and katakana.

Interested in joining our Japanese Crash Course, or wondering if it’s the right fit for you? We’d love to help! Simply fill out the contact form below, and our English-speaking staff will get back to you shortly.


Get In Touch With Our Team!


What is Japanese Crash Course?

Coto Academy’s Japanese Crash Course is an intensive, short-term survival program designed specifically for complete beginners and new residents in Japan who need to build functional, everyday Japanese skills as quickly as possible.

AspectDetails

Target LevelZero Beginner (No prior Japanese knowledge required)

Duration1 to 4 weeks (standard core unit runs 4 weeks)

SchedulePart-time intensive (e.g., 4 days/week, 2 hours/day)

LocationsCoto Academy locations (such as Azabu, Iidabashi, Yokohama) & Online

Key Features & Learning Focus


Practical, Conversation-First Curriculum: Focuses on immediate, practical communication rather than heavy grammar theory. Students master key phrases across 9 real-life scenarios, including ordering at restaurants, shopping, asking for directions, self-introductions, and simple daily interactions.

Basic Literacy: Teaches Hiragana and Katakana reading and writing, alongside common Kanji frequently encountered in daily life (such as street signs, menus, and shop notices).

Small Class Sizes: Limited to a maximum of 8 students per class (averaging 3–6), ensuring maximum speaking time and individual feedback from instructors.

Experiential Learning (Tokyo Explorer): Includes interactive outdoor activities where students put their classroom learning to the test in real-world settings like local cafes, supermarkets, and izakayas.


How is Japanese Crash Course Different From Beginner Japanese Lessons?

Japanese Crash Course is a special course designed for individuals who have completely zero knowledge or prior experience in learning Japanese. On the other hand, some beginner Japanese lessons might already expect students to know about basic hiragana and katakana and phrases.

It is important to clarify with your chosen Japanese language school if the beginner lessons they offer are designed for total beginners or not.

Who is This Japanese Crash Course For?

Other than for total beginners, we think Japanese Crash Course is the right fit for you if you:

1. New Arrivals Who Want Practical, Everyday Japanese

If you just arrived in Japan and need to start communicating right away, this course prioritizes real-life interaction over dry theory. Rather than spending weeks on abstract grammar rules, you learn functional phrases you can use immediately for shopping, ordering food, and navigating daily life. The speaking-first approach gets you talking from day one so you feel confident handling everyday tasks.

2. Returning Learners Rebuilding Their Foundation

If you studied Japanese before but took a long break, this course serves as an efficient refresher. It helps you clean up forgotten grammar, review Hiragana and Katakana, and fix gaps in your foundational skills. This reactivates your speaking momentum without forcing you into an overly advanced class.

3. Short-Term Visitors, Tourists & Travelers

If you are visiting Japan for a few weeks or months, you can enjoy a flexible language immersion experience without long-term commitments. Unlike traditional language schools that require 6-month or 1-year visa commitments, you can enroll for short blocks starting from just 1 week. It offers a hands-on way to make your trip richer by learning the language while exploring the country.

What’s The Experiential Learning at Coto Academy’s Japanese Crash Course?

At Coto Academy, we believe learning a language shouldn’t feel like studying for a history exam. Japanese is a living, breathing tool, and you should get to use it from day one!

That’s where Experiential Learning comes in. Once a week, we take the learning outside! Guided by your teacher, you’ll head out of our campus to complete fun missions like ordering a customized drink, asking a shopkeeper for recommendations, or getting directions to a nearby landmark.

Inside the class, you can expect role-plays like introducing yourself to new friends and handling shopping questions.

Ready to Start Your Japanese Journey?

If you’re excited to learn Japanese by actually living it, our Japanese Crash Course is ready for you! Classes run in small groups to make sure everyone gets plenty of speaking time and personal guidance.

Come join us, meet fellow learners from around the world, and start exploring Japan with confidence!


Contact Us and Start Learning Japanese!


FAQ

Do I need any prior Japanese knowledge to join this course?

No prior experience is necessary! The Japanese Crash Course is specially designed for absolute beginners (Zero Beginner). Whether you haven’t learned a single word yet or only know konnichiwa, our native teachers will walk you through daily essential phrases, as well as hiragana and katakana, step by step.

How long does the course last, and how flexible is the schedule?

We offer high flexibility so you don’t need to make a long-term commitment. While the core unit runs for 4 weeks, you can enroll for anywhere from 1 week to 12 weeks depending on your availability and length of stay in Japan. Classes typically run part-time multiple days a week, making it easy to fit into a busy schedule.

What is the class size like?

To ensure everyone gets personal attention and plenty of speaking time, our classes are kept strictly small, with a maximum of 8 students per class (averaging around 3 to 6 students). You will have continuous opportunities to practice active conversation rather than just passively listening to a lecture.

items.text:
The new Street Fighter movie (dir. Kitao Sakurai) that opened on October 16 seemingly has one of the easiest jobs in the world. Not only is it based on Capcom’s bestselling fighting game franchise in a time when video game adaptations have proven themselves to be commercially and artistically viable, the bar that the film has to clear is Street Fighter (1994). For years considered one of the worst movies ever made, reactions to it have softened over the years but, at best, they basically boil down to “so bad, it’s kind of good.” And if being better than Steven E. de Souza’s film is a mark of success, then Sakurai’s Street Fighter has already won because it’s not bad. It’s good. Even great at times. But that may not matter, at least for Japan. There are a lot of factors at play here.

VIDEO

For Japan, the Movie to Beat Wasn’t the 1994 Adaptation

Japanese audiences did not love Steven E. de Souza’s Street Fighter, but they also didn’t despise it. There were criticisms at shifting the focus away from Ryu and Ken to the American character Guile (Jean-Claude Van Damme), the B-movie feel of it all and the militaristic guns-blazing vibe to the story. The last one is a common and understandable admonition of the film from a country that still deals with monstrous behavior by some members of the US military. But praise was occasionally given to the scope of the 1994 film as well as some of its sets, effects and performances.

The first Street Fighter adaptation is certified “rotten” on Rotten Tomatoes with a score of 20% from both audiences and critics. But Japanese review sites like KINENOTE or Eiga.com give it a much more lenient 51.5/100 and 2.7/5, respectively. That might be because, before watching Steven E. de Souza’s take on the Capcom property, Japan was treated to what many still consider the best possible adaptation of Street Fighter.

Street Fighter II: The Animated Movie (dir. Gisaburo Sugii) premiered in 1994, a year before the live-action movie was released in Japan. It was a critical and box office success fueled by its faithfulness to the Street Fighter lore and amazing animation. This is the movie that still lives in the pop-culture memory of Japan over 30 years later. This is the movie that Sakurai’s Street Fighter is secretly competing with to attract Japanese fans of the games. And it really did try its hardest.

VIDEO

Street Fighter 2026 Is Uniquely Tailored to Japanese Audiences

Sakurai’s Street Fighter is a live-action movie, but it’s bookended by animated sequences that also pop up throughout the film, courtesy of Titmouse Inc. The scenes are really beautiful, with amazing, fast-paced action. They also technically make a lot of sense since most of the animated parts are flashbacks, which meant that the movie didn’t have to go looking for additional co-stars to play the young Ryu and Ken.

The sequences additionally include a character who might become a big part of the franchise in the future, and introducing him via animation with no lines opens up casting options for a possible sequel. But it still feels like chunks of Street Fighter (2026) are animated to make fans of Street Fighter II: The Animated Movie happy.

Honda and even features a prolonged dialogue scene entirely in Japanese. And throughout it all, it doesn’t for one second alienate American viewers.

A Love Letter to the Games

While Koji’s Ryu is one of the central characters of Street Fighter (2026), the movie’s heart is the character’s partner Ken, played by Noah Centineo in a performance of a lifetime. Bison is also phenomenal, bringing a wonderfully creepy cult leader energy to the big screen, as well as Raúl Juliá’s famous “Tuesday” line from the 1994 film (if you know, you know).
